state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Why do you think Fido falling asleep would result in a negative-sloping section on the graph? Can you think of any other reasons why the distance might be decreasing in that part of the graph?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess if Fido was falling asleep, he wouldn't really be moving, but I still don’t get why the line goes down. Maybe it means he’s going back home? But how does that work if he was just running away? I'm a bit confused about how the graph shows movement and rest.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: If Fido was running away from home, would he be getting closer or farther away from home? How does that relate to the direction of the line on the graph? Let's think about how distance and movement are connected in this situation.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think if Fido was running away, he would be getting farther from home, so the line should go up, right? But if the line goes down, maybe it means he’s coming back? I’m still not sure how to tell when he’s resting or moving just by looking at the graph. Can you help me understand that better?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher asks probing questions but never directly addresses the student's core confusion about distinguishing rest (horizontal line) from movement (sloped line), and while the student makes progress on understanding the negative slope means returning home, they explicitly state they still don't understand how to identify rest versus movement by Turn 4.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's reasoning without ever directly stating the answer, exemplifying the Socratic method throughout all interactions.
